subject: Career
title: Social Capital: The Currency of Connections
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Social Capital: The Currency of Connections.

hook.text: Two people apply for the same job. One has a referral. She gets the interview. That's social capital.

buildup.text: Sociologist Pierre Bourdieu defined social capital as resources gained through relationships.

discovery.text: Unlike financial capital, social capital grows when you spend it. Helping others increases your value.

twist.text: But it's not infinite. Burning trust through bad referrals depletes your social capital fast.

climax.text: Social capital compounds: good connections lead to more good connections over time.

punchline.text: Your network is your net worth — in more ways than money.

quiz.question: Who defined social capital as resources gained through relationships?

details.summary: Social capital is the value derived from your network of relationships, including trust, reciprocity, and access to information. Like financial capital, it can be built, invested, spent, and depleted through strategic or careless actions.
details.whyItMatters: Careers advance through relationships as much as competence. Social capital determines who gets opportunities, referrals, and insider knowledge that formal channels cannot provide.
takeaways: Social capital includes bonding, bridging, and linking types
Trust is the foundational currency that enables all network value
Social capital depreciates without regular maintenance

faq.question: What is the difference between bonding and bridging social capital?
faq.answer: Bonding social capital exists within tight-knit groups like close colleagues or industry peers. Bridging social capital spans across different groups, connecting you to diverse communities. Bridging capital is rarer and typically more valuable for career advancement.

faq.question: Can introverts build strong social capital in their careers?
faq.answer: Absolutely. Introverts often build deeper, higher-quality connections through one-on-one conversations and thoughtful follow-ups. Social capital is about depth and trust, not the number of superficial connections, which plays to introverted strengths.
